Data Engineering Design Patterns

Bartosz Konieczny

A catalogue of about 70 reusable solutions to recurring data engineering problems — subtitled Recipes for Solving the Most Common Data Engineering Problems. Each pattern follows the same shape: a problem, a solution, its consequences and runnable examples (mostly Apache Spark, Delta Lake, Apache Kafka, Apache Airflow, PostgreSQL and the major clouds). The chapters follow data through a platform: ingestion, error management, idempotency, adding value, orchestrating flows, security, storage, quality and observability. A blog analytics platform serves as the running case study.

How the book fits together

The book has no part divisions. Chapter 1 orders the pattern chapters along a typical data flow, and this map follows that order. The grouping into three stages is the vault's own.

Some threads run across the groups:

  • Partitioning (8) underpins the Fast Metadata Cleaner (4) and incremental loading (2).
  • The Dead-Letter (3) returns as data dispatching in AWAP (9).
  • The Vertical Partitioner appears for removal (7) and for storage (8).
  • The Readiness Marker (2) gates the Skew Detector (10).
  • The Fine-Grained Tracker (10) supports the Schema Migrator (9).

Simulations

Interactive models of the mechanisms the book describes. They are embedded in the lessons too; implementations are the vault’s own.

  • Chapter 2Small files and compactionStream 10-minute micro-batches into a table for 90 days, watch the daily batch job's file overhead grow, and compare compaction schedules and vacuum retention.
  • Chapter 2Incremental loading and backfillsRun hourly incremental loads with an unbounded delta column, a bounded delta column or time partitions, then hard-delete rows and backfill old hours to see what each implementation reads and misses.
  • Chapter 3Watermarks and late dataReplay the book's Table 3-1 and Table 3-2 event streams, change the allowed lateness and the window size, and see which events are ignored and when windows are emitted.
  • Chapter 4Merger vs Stateful MergerReplay the book's A/B/C/M/N/O increments with a plain MERGE and with a state table that restores the right version before backfilling, and compare what consumers see during the replay.
  • Chapter 5Bin packing vs partial commitsDeliver per-partner aggregates in event-time order to a broker with partial-commit semantics, one record at a time, in naive bulk requests, or in bins with at most one record per key, and see which keys end up out of order.
  • Chapter 6Single vs concurrent runnerSchedule hourly runs, stretch their duration past the hour, and compare how delays accumulate when only one run may execute at a time and when several may run concurrently.
  • Chapter 8Bucket pruning and Z-order skippingHash keys into buckets to see bucket pruning and shuffle-free joins, then lay out a two-column dataset lexicographically or in Z-order and count the data blocks a query must read using per-block min/max statistics.
  • Chapter 9Schema compatibility checkerEvolve the book's Order and Visit schemas, pick backward, forward or full compatibility, transitive or not, and see which reader versions can read which writer versions and which changes a registry rejects.

Key concepts

These ideas recur across chapters; each row lists the chapters that discuss it. Definitions are the vault's summaries of the book's explanations.

ConceptDefinitionChapters
BackfillingReprocessing past data, for example after fixing a bug or adding a consumer. Many patterns are judged by what they do when old runs are replayed.2 · 4 · 6
Dead-letter storageA separate place for records that fail processing, so the pipeline keeps going and the failures can be inspected and replayed.1 · 3 · 9
IdempotencyGetting the same result however many times a job runs for the same input, whether through overwrites, merges, keys, transactions or proxies.3 · 4 · 7 · 8
Late dataEvents that arrive after the system expected them, measured against a watermark. Late events can be dropped, integrated statically or integrated dynamically.3 · 5 · 10
Medallion architectureOrganizing data in Bronze (raw), Silver (cleaned, enriched) and Gold (business-ready) layers. The case study uses it throughout.1 · 2 · 5
PartitioningSplitting a dataset into separate storage locations by rows (horizontal) or columns (vertical), so readers and cleaners touch only what they need.2 · 4 · 7 · 8
Personal data (PII)Information that identifies a person, which privacy laws let users have removed and which must be protected or (pseudo-)anonymized before it is shared.2 · 7
Schema evolutionChanges to a dataset's structure over time. Compatibility rules and grace periods keep consumers working through those changes.9 · 10
ShuffleMoving data across the network so that records with the same key meet in one task, as aggregations and joins require. It is often the costliest step.5 · 8
Slowly changing dimensionA way of keeping the history of reference data that changes over time, so facts join with the version valid at their time.5 · 8
Small files problemMany tiny files cost more in listing and metadata than they hold in data. Compaction, partition choice and manifests address it.2 · 8 · 10
Table file formatsDelta Lake, Apache Iceberg and Apache Hudi: Parquet files plus a commit log that adds transactions, time travel, statistics and file manifests.2 · 4 · 7 · 8
WatermarkA pipeline's estimate of how far event time has progressed. It decides when windows close and which events count as late.3 · 5
